utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic, and Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I welcome you all, and I welcome you as well. I want to make sure, first and foremost, that you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand, so I will start with you, Mr. Mrksic. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radic, can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand? THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Sljivancanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand? THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you all. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'm Patricia Sellers representing the Prosecution today, assisted by co-counsel Kristina Carey, Joanne Richardson, and our case manager is Diane Boles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What happened to Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben is on mission this week, and he'll return to the office on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's still in the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, he is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure. I thank you, madam, and good afternoon. Appearances for accused Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Defence for General Mile Mrksic is Mr. Miroslav Vasic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Vasic, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Mr. Radic will be represented by Ms. Tapuskovic, attorney from Belgrade, as co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all the parties in the proceedings. Mr. Sljivancanin will be represented today by Mr. Novak Lukic, as lead counsel, and Mr. Momcilo Bulatovic is also present in the courtroom as co-counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you both. Mr. Borovic is still in the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but this time Mr. Borovic has decided that I should be present at this Status Conference today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So just for formality's sake, may I repeat once more what the purpose of the Status Conference is. You will all recall that the last Status Conference was held on the 16th of February of this year, and in terms of Rule 65 bis, the Pre-Trial Judge is bound to reconvene another -- to convene another Status Conference within 120 days after the last Status Conference. I have convened the Status Conference for today, and in terms of Rule 65 bis, the purpose is to organise exchanges between the parties, with a view to ensuring an expeditious preparation for the trial, and I must say that in this respect and the past Status Conference, I have had full cooperation from both sides, which I appreciate, and also to allow, give an opportunity to the accused to raise any matter in relation to the mental and physical condition. And in this, I also usually include the condition of detention as it relates to detention. You are aware that in preparation for this particular -- you're not hearing? THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have no translation. Is it okay now? THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] It's all right now, Your Honour. I can hear it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I will just read out what I said already for your benefit. I was explaining what the purpose of this Status Conference is, a Status Conference which is being convened within the 120-day period laid down by Rule 65 bis, following the last Status Conference, the purpose being to organise exchanges between the parties so as to ensure an expeditious preparation for trial, and secondly, to give you, each one of you, the opportunity to raise any issue in relation to your mental and physical condition, as well as your conditions of detention. You are also aware that in preparation for this particular Status Conference, I authorised my Senior Legal Officer to hold a 65 ter meeting with the lawyers, Prosecution and Defence, in preparation for this Status Conference. The 65 ter meeting was held on Wednesday of this week, on the 9th, at 11.00 in the morning. Several issues were raised during this 65 ter meeting, some of which I will be referring to very briefly as we go along, and we will only concentrate on those issues that were not accompanied with a conclusion during this 65 ter meeting. But I will mention what was discussed for your sake, because obviously you were not present for this meeting. I will start with the outstanding motions. There was an outstanding motion on the level of the case. I have been informed that this has now been decided by the Registrar precisely today. I don't know if you are aware of the decision. You are not aware -- Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately, we still have not been informed about that. We did check our lockers today, but we did not find that decision there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision which your client -- upon the motion that your client filed. Mr. Roberts, can you check --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm being informed that actually it's not a decision which is being filed; it's a decision which is being communicated to you individually, either to your clients or to you directly. I think, Mr. Vasic, it's Mr. -- either you or your client. I wouldn't know exactly. We were told that it would be communicated to you before the sitting. I can't say that it hasn't been, because I don't know whether you have checked your letter box. So but I am informing you that based on the information that I have, the decision has been taken and that it has been or should be communicated to you today. And I'm sure you will know how to regulate yourself after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will be expecting the decision, and thank you for informing us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then there is a request by accused Radic, based on his partial indigence. Basically, just to inform also the public, on the 27th of October of last year, counsel for accused Radic submitted a request to review the Registrar's decision of October 7 of the same year, which, inter alia, states that the accused should bear the costs associated with 223 hours of investigative and legal assistance work at the pre-trial stage. The Radic Defence, in its motion, requested the Trial Chamber to rule that the cost of 223 hours of investigative work at the pre-trial Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stage be instead borne by the Tribunal. By order of the Trial Chamber, the Registry filed comments and associated material on this matter on the motion on the 12th of January of this year. It also requested the Trial Chamber to deny the accused's motion and to confirm the Registrar's decision on partial indigence of the accused. Defence counsel for Radic responded on the 26th of February -- of January, 2004, maintaining its position, and reiterating its request to the Trial Chamber to accept -- uphold the motion and review the Registrar's decision. There's nothing much has happened after this. In view of the implementation by OLAD of a new system of legal aid, as of the beginning of May, the question was raised by the senior -- by my Senior Legal Officer during the 65 ter meeting you had two days ago with a view to exploring together with you whether this new system could impact -- have an impact on the Registrar's decision. I am informed by my Senior Legal Officer that co-counsel for Mr. Radic indicated that there had indeed been an impact on the Sljivancanin case and that they were simply waiting for a decision before taking any further steps. We are, or rather, I am watching the situation and will be following this matter up with the Senior Legal Officer, with whom I have had very little chance to converse after this 65 ter meeting because of other matters that I was attending and he was attending too. This matter will receive my utmost attention and I will pursue it and hand down the decision at the earliest. Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- excuse me just for a minute, because it seems there aren't enough microphones. At the 65 ter Conference, we only slightly touched upon this matter. The new policy of appointing an official counsel, Defence counsel, went into force on the 4th of May of this year, and on the same day, the Registrar made a new revised decision regarding the accused Sljivancanin. We all received a kind of form explaining how this new policy works at the Tribunal, the policy of appointing a counsel. However, at the moment, this is a policy that should be applied to new cases. Of course, we will leave that up to the Chamber and to the Registrar to decide whether a new amended indictment would count as a new case when we are talking about the appointment of a defence counsel to an accused. We believe that it would be too early to decide in any way whether the new policy is something that can be applied to the rest of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Tapuskovic. Tapuskovic. Pardon me if I sometimes mess up the names. As I said, I will pursue the matter and we'll deal with it, and hopefully the position should -- will have crystallised or should crystallise before the next Status Conference. I do not anticipate this to drag on indefinitely. There is a third motion, which is very important, a motion which refers -- goes back to accused Mrksic and Sljivancanin. And for the record, I will just state for the time being that initially it was accused Mrksic who started the ball rolling, and on the 12th of March of this year, through his counsel, he filed a preliminary motion challenging several defects in the form of the modified consolidated amended indictment, issued on the 9th of February, 2004. This motion challenging the indictment, the consolidated, amended indictment, was followed by a response which was filed by the Prosecution on the 25th of March, 2004. Now, at the same time, on the 11th of March, counsel for Sljivancanin also filed a preliminary motion challenging as well certain defects in the form of the modified, consolidated, amended indictment, and the matter, or the motion was responded to by the Prosecution on the same day as in the case of Mrksic, that is, on the 25th of March, 2004. As you know, this matter is still pending. It requires certain attention, more than under normal circumstances. And I am informed that in the course of the 65 ter meeting you had, Mr. Von Hebel, as the Senior Legal Officer, informed you, Mr. Vasic, and you, Mr. Bulatovic or Mr. Lukic, whoever of you was present, that the matter is still pending. We are giving it some attention. We are not -- we have not yet started giving it full attention. It requires both myself, the other two Judges, as well as Mr. Von Hebel and the rest of the staff, to concentrate fully on it. It requires a lot of attention, as I explained, and at the moment I am engaged in the process of elaborating the judgement in the Brdjanin case and the drafting, and I will continue to be so engaged until the end of August. However, I do have someone dealing precisely -- in fact, I have two, one legal officer and one intern, researching the matters that you have raised. I cannot report to you any significant progress, but as soon as we are in a position to engage ourselves fully in it, we will then hopefully come back to you with our decision. But that's the position. I'm being very frank with you. Judge Parker is reaching the final stages in his case. I have reached the final stages in my case. Mr. Von Hebel is dealing with all the three Judges, plus the other Judges in Trial Chamber II, and he is up to his neck with work. The rest of our staff are engaged in the drafting process and in the research process. We can't work out miracles. My apologies to you, but we are doing our best. And I would close this chapter here on motions. Are there any comments that either -- from your side, Madam Prosecutor, or from your side, Defence counsel, you would like to raise, or motions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have no comments pertaining to motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we do not have anything to add, Your Honour. Thank you very much for informing us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have already said what I meant to say about the motion regarding the work of the investigators. Since the accused Radic has not objected to the indictment again, we have nothing further to say on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And I suppose the same applies to you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have no further objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you all. And I will open the discussion on disclosures. I propose to deal with the different types of disclosures that are dealt with by our Rules, starting with Rule 66(A), paragraph (i) material. I am informed, but please correct me if I'm wrong, that defence counsel for the three accused have agreed that the material that should have been disclosed under this particular paragraph, part of Rule 66, has indeed been disclosed to each and every one of you. I can refer you to transcript pages 80 and 113, and the 65 ter meeting that was convened on my instructions, upon my instructions, way back in October of 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that also applies to all of the defence teams. I just want to make things a little bit shorter. My colleagues have authorised me to speak on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we then come next to statements which fall under paragraph (ii) of part A of Rule 66. And I refer you to a partially confidential Prosecution's first report concerning disclosure. I need not go into much detail, especially since it is partially confidential. You will recall that this was filed on the 1st of April, 2003. Prosecution did not mean to play a joke on anyone. It was not an April fool's report, first report. And it detailed in its confidential attachment the materials disclosed to the defence counsel for the three accused. At the time, accused Sljivancanin, I think, was still unrepresented. The Prosecution has since -- at least, this is what I am Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. informed -- has since assured counsel for accused Sljivancanin that the material which he received from his client was the same that had been disclosed pursuant to the relevant Rules, including Rule 68, to counsel for the other two accused. I want to confirm that this is so and that you are happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Madam Tapuskovic, the same?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I expected my colleague to confirm that, since we already exchanged information and have confirmed that we all received the same sets of material from the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's important, especially from the Sljivancanin defence, I think. Then at the 16th of February of this year, we had the last Status Conference, as I explained earlier, and the Prosecution informed that it had disclosed the statements or testimonies or evidence of 23 witnesses from its ongoing witness list, which at the time, Madam Sellers declared that it contained something like anything between 60 and 80 witnesses at the time. I don't know if the situation, the position is still the same. Prosecution, at the -- during that Status Conference, stressed that the case had not yet been prioritised with the Evidence Unit but that they would do their level best, they would endeavour to at least turn over the statements of witnesses that have previously testified before this Tribunal, including, in order to do so, seeking variation of protective measures when applicable. The Defence for all three accused considered the extent of this disclosure to be insufficient at that stage. This was in February. And so we will need to update ourselves on the situation. At the time, I had encouraged or exhorted the Prosecution to accelerate the process, as you will recall, process of disclosure, and I had pointed out that an assessment of the situation of this disclosure will be made today. Of course, I realise, I am fully aware, that much will depend on the progress made until now, and that I had indicated that if I had reason to feel unhappy with the process -- with the progress made, then I was reserving for myself the right to fix a time limit within which the Prosecution would then fulfil its disclosure obligations. I am informed by Mr. Von Hebel that the issues rising out of Rule 66(A)(ii) was addressed in detail. I'm told in the course of the -- last Wednesday's 65 ter meeting, during which the Prosecution provided an update on its disclosure activities since the February Status Conference. I am informed - again, I stand to be corrected - that effectively the Prosecution has disclosed further statements of nine -- nine further witness statements. If the arithmetic of the Trial Chamber is correct, this basically means that the Prosecution has now disclosed 31 of a total of about 53 to 55 statements for witnesses expected to be called. For the remaining 22 statements, roughly, I am told that the Prosecution will be filing protective measures prior to disclosure. Prosecution, in the course of the 65 ter meeting, also clarified that they expect to add a few witnesses from those who are presently testifying in the Ovcara trial. You are fully familiar with the Ovcara trial, Mr. Radic, Mr. Mrksic, and Mr. Sljivancanin. I don't think I need to explain what I'm talking about. If I need to, please let me know. Okay. Taking place in Serbia. So far, I will stop here for the time being. Is there anything in the statement that I have made that anyone of you would like to correct? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. The Prosecution believes that that is an accurate reflection of what was discussed in the 65 ter and the actual state of our disclosure obligation under 66(A).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Sellers. The same with the Defence. If I see no objection, I take it that -- yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This indicates that obviously we have made some headway in terms of discovery. The only thing that perplexes the Defence is the discovery of the 26th of April, 2004. There are 208 statements. But a lot of material was supplied to the Defence, according to Rule 66 and Rule 68 at the same time. So perhaps after the Status Conference, the Defence teams could meet with our colleagues from the Prosecution to look through the names of the 31 witnesses whose statements were disclosed to us. Because, as I said, the material was disclosed to us in accordance with two different Rules. That is the only thing that perplexes the Defence at this point, and I say this again on behalf of all three Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to add one more thing. So far we have received from the Prosecution three reports on disclosure. These are very useful documents for the Defence. The last report was received in the month of October. We expected to get one perhaps prior to this Status Conference because some progress had been made in this disclosure and discovery process. We would appreciate it if the Prosecution could keep us abreast of things, perhaps not only on the eve of Status Conferences, so that the teams could collate documentation amongst themselves and that we could communicate with the Prosecution and establish the exact quantity of the disclosed materials. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Tapuskovic. In fact, what you stated, and particularly what you, Mr. Vasic, stated, leads me straight into the next point that I have included in the agenda following the report made to me by Mr. Von Hebel. I am informed, indeed, that in the course of the 65 ter meeting, your perplexity was -- as to whether certain statements were being disclosed under Rule 66 or under Rule 68 was made clear, and I have the following note, which I have based on Mr. Von Hebel's information or report. Defence counsel raised the issue that there seems to be confusion about whether statements are being disclosed pursuant to Rule 66 or Rule 68. I am also informed that this was highlighted as being an important issue because of the priority which must be assigned to the translation of 66 -- Rule 66(A)(ii) statements. But I am also informed that the Prosecution clarified in the course of the 65 ter meeting that the 31 witness statements disclosed to date were all disclosed pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii), as distinguished from the statements and documents from the Ovcara trial, which were disclosed pursuant to Rule 68. I will come to these even later on. I have taken note of what you have stated. If you still see the utility of having a short, informal meeting with the Prosecution after the Status Conference, I am sure that there will be full cooperation from the Prosecution, because this is a matter that, if clarified further, would only benefit the Trial Chamber. So I encourage you, if there is still -- I exhort you, if there is still any confusion in the minds of the Defence, to clear that up with them following the Status Conference, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'd be more than willing to meet with our colleagues to clarify any other disclosure issues, including the ones that are before us right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And again, you will have noticed that I combined the issue of disclosure under 66 rather than under 68 in connection with translation problems, which, as you are aware, this case is facing. I am informed, and I'm not happy with the situation, but I'm also aware that this is not something which is unique to this case, but it is also applicable to other cases pending before this Tribunal, the issue of translation of disclosed documents was raised, and it was submitted that it is critical. Counsel for Mr. Radic noted that of the nine witness statements recently disclosed pursuant to -- the nine witness statements I mentioned earlier, only one had been provided in B/C/S. The Defence counsel complained that this is causing delays for the Defence because counsel, of course, is required to provide his client or her client with the translation and then even enter into some kind of discussion with the client on the contents of the statement. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. If this has to be done before the translation is effectively provided, it entails a lot of work on the part of the Defence. It's not practical. So my concern is that this matter is given priority, it is prioritised, so as to allay the concerns of the defence teams and also lessen the burden that each one of them has to carry. There is another aspect which was raised during the 65 ter meeting, which I frankly was tempted not to refer to. But if the situation remains as it is, there is another problem. If the Defence -- if defence counsel are necessarily engaged in this additional work that they have to undertake in order to keep their clients posted with the contents of these statements, it seems that the matter cannot be brought up with the Registrar as forming the basis for a claim for compensation. Of course, I mean, I do not have any power to interfere with the discretion that is reserved under our law, under our Statute and our Rules to the Registrar. On the other hand, it's not fair that the defence counsel are put in that position, or if they are already in that position, that this situation is prolonged much further. So what I am going to suggest to you is this: In between Status Conferences, you, in particular, Prosecution, are in a much better position than I am to make an assessment of what the likely progress is, or what -- where we stand, in other words. The same applies to you. If the situation is protracted, is prolonged, and we approach the next Status Conference with you receiving further statements without the previous one having been translated, I invite you both to file either a report or a motion to me, and then I will provide as necessary. For the time being, I'm not going to do so, because I do not have concrete information that would strengthen my hand and justify my handing down an order. But if the situation gets worse or doesn't get any better, then I want to know so that I will intervene within the powers that are reserved for me as the Pre-Trial Judge in these and other matters. So do I get my message home? Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on behalf of all three defence teams, I wish to thank you for this approach of yours to this subject which is of such great importance to us. We will do our best to follow matters in cooperation with the Prosecution. We understand how busy they are too. I wish to remind you of another thing that is related to this subject matter. From the Prosecution, we received all the transcripts of the Dokmanovic trial. We got them from the Prosecution, and of course there's no need for me to explain how valuable they are to us. We ourselves interpret the transcripts to our clients. That's what we mentioned at the 65 ter meeting. Every translation of documents into B/C/S makes our work much, much easier and we have such a great deal of work anyway, as we explained to the Registry. You know that the Trial Chamber of the Milosevic trial will give us the Milosevic trial documents as well, and we have to analyse them together with our clients. So that is what I wanted to highlight so that you would understand the importance of receiving as many documents as possible in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I was coming to the Dokmanovic documents, because I have full information on what went on during the 65 ter meeting. And it is precisely also because of what you have just mentioned about this that I am refraining from making any orders today. Because, as I said, I usually look well before I jump, before I leap, because I want to make sure what is involved. If we're talking of a few pages, from my experience here in these past two and a half years plus, when it's necessary, all the translation units will come forward. They are very cooperative, extremely cooperative, considering the amount of work and the burden that they have to carry, and they try, do their level best, to keep us happy. Of course, there are limits. I cannot explain -- I cannot expect to impose on them beyond what they can actually carry. However, it can become a question of prioritising, and in that case we will have to see precisely where we stand vis-a-vis other cases as well and vis-a-vis other translations for other cases that are being undertaken. What I promise you is that I will do my best to try and lessen your burden, and also the burden of the Prosecution arising from their duty to disclose. There is a further matter that was discussed within the context of disclosure during the 65 ter meeting, which I am not that clear in my mind as to what went on and what was agreed. I have on record from Mr. Von Hebel that the Prosecution, apart from undertaking to establish and to what extent translation of the 31 disclosed statements has been provided and to follow up with respect to the Dokmanovic statements that you pointed out, Prosecution then requested the Defence to make available to it any material which any of the three teams managed to obtain from the military archives. Perhaps you could enlighten me on this particular matter. This is all the information I have. As I told you, I haven't had time to go any deeper with Mr. Von Hebel. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to say that that was a comment that was made in the spirit of colleague cooperation, but I would suggest that that's something that we discuss with the defence counsel possibly in the meeting after our hearing before you today. And, Your Honour, we would get back to you if there's anything that the Trial Chamber should be appraised of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Is That agreeable, Mr. Vasic, Madam Tapuskovic, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence was taken aback a bit by what our learned friends of the Prosecution said. First of all, because things are being put as if the Defence has these documents from the military archives. I don't know where my learned friend get that kind of information from. Secondly, on which basis could the Prosecution seek these documents at this stage of the proceedings? So we are taken aback by this, namely, taking as a matter of fact that the Defence has these documents. Could our learned friends of the Prosecution please put this in writing and tell us where they get these sources from. So could we learn how they ask us to do this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This subject was raised at the 65 ter meeting when I presented our problems that we have in relation to the National Council for Cooperation with the Hague Tribunal and the possibility for the defence to get the documents it seeks through official channels. But I must say that I was taken aback by the position of the Prosecution because, as far as I know, not a single Defence is at the stage of reciprocal disclosure. So even if I did have some documents now, unless we went into reciprocal disclosure, why would I have to disclose anything now? This was a technical objection because I saw that the Prosecution did receive from the Belgrade court the Belgrade trial, the Ovcara trial, if I can put it that way, they received these documents in English, so we asked them to give us these transcripts in B/C/S so that we can have the same thing. And that is what was derived from the documents that they gave us. However my position is that even if I did have some documents and if I'm not in the process of reciprocal discovery, I really have no obligation in the pre-trial stage to give the Prosecution any documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, you know what the position with regard to reciprocal disclosure was under the Rules and how it is now, and things may also change in the very near future. I will not comment any further on this matter. The Trial Chamber is not seized with any motion. It's just information that I have on a subject that was discussed during the 65 ter meeting, and I registered that there was disagreement on this matter. I will pronounce myself alone as Pre-Trial Judge or collectively with the other two Judges, depending on whether there will be an ad hoc motion. Yes. If there can be one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Might I take the floor for a second. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I would just like to reiterate that we have not put anywhere on the record or in any way think that the Defence at this time is in possession of any of these documents. I would certainly want to make that clear. And certainly agree that we can discuss this matter. I would also like to inform the Trial Chamber that the issue of documents in the original language was raised by our learned colleagues and I believe today that we have been able to provide them with all of those documents in the original language, and we certainly hope that that will assist your ability to represent your clients. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Disclosure under Rule 67, which, as you know, has been amended. 65 -- Rule 67, which was amended way back during the plenary, during the December plenary, and which deals with additional disclosure, provides, inter alia, that within a time limit established by the Trial Chamber or by the Trial Judge, the Defence shall notify the Prosecution of its intent to offer the defence of alibi and any special defence. In addition, a new paragraph has been included in the Rules, providing that if either party discovers additional evidence or material which should have been disclosed earlier pursuant to the Rules, that party shall immediately disclose that evidence or material to the other party and the Trial Chamber, and the Trial Chamber. I am informed that nothing was discussed relating to Rule 67 during the 65 ter meeting. I would like you to confirm this, first and foremost, and then to indicate whether you would like to discuss anything in the context of this particular Rule. Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I confirm that there was no discussion on Rule 67 at the 65 ter meeting and I would just like to briefly speak with my colleagues prior to responding to the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. In the meantime, I can consult the three Defence counsel. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to confirm what my learned friend said. Rule 67 disclosure was not mentioned during the 65 ter Conference, and the position of the Defence teams is that we cannot discuss this subject until the indictment is not in place, until the preliminary motions are not resolved, and only then we can take a position regarding this kind of disclosure with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the position of Ms. Tapuskovic and Mr. Lukic the same? Okay. I think that is a reasonable approach on the part of the Defence. There is an important motion dealing with the indictment which is still pending. Disclosure is not yet complete. And I think it would be premature on my part, or on your part, to insist on establishing a time limit under Rule 67 for the time being. Ms. Sellers, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would agree with the position both of the Trial Chamber and our colleagues. We would also like to reiterate that we understand that we still are in pre-trial in terms of the indictment has not been completely confirmed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that is perfect. Thank you. And I come to disclosure under Rule 68, which, as you know, has also been the subject of some amendments and which probably again will be the subject of further amendments within a month's time. Rule 68 provides, inter alia, that the Prosecution shall, as soon as practicable, disclose to the Defence any material which, in the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor - this may change - may suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence, and secondly, the Prosecution shall make available to the Defence in an electronic form collections of relevant material held by it, together with appropriate computer software with which the Defence can search such collections electronically. The Prosecution, as I explained earlier, within this context, filed, on the 1st of August of last year, a first report concerning disclosure, which was partially confidential. I have already referred to it before. Then she followed up with a second report concerning disclosure. This was filed on the 4th of September. And then we had a final -- or an additional third, partially confidential report concerning disclosure, to which Ms. Tapuskovic referred to, which was filed on the 21st of October. These three reports detail the material disclosed pursuant to Rule 68 to the three accused so far. Now, you will recall that when we had the last Status Conference way back in February, 16th of February, and Rule 68 had already been amended, I had expressed what I understood to be an ongoing exercise at the time of disclosure, and I also tried to emphasise that it was important, in my mind at least, to draw a distinction between the s the exculpatory material proper, which is specifically dealt with by one part of Rule 68, and the rest of the material to be disclosed, which was not previously dealt with by Rule 68 but which is now specifically dealt with by Rule 68. The two are quite different. I would say they are radically different. We had agreed at the time that I was going to leave you free completely, particularly the Prosecution, to make an assessment of the situation as it emerged from a proper reading of Rule 68 and that you would report back to the Trial Chamber today. I am informed by Mr. Von Hebel that in the course of the 65 ter meeting, you, Ms. Sellers, or whoever was present - I don't know whether you were all there or whether some of you were there - you confirmed that 75 documents and 14 statements from witnesses from the Ovcara trial currently taking place in Serbia had been disclosed pursuant to Rule 68. These statements, according to what is being reported back to me by Mr. Von Hebel, and in answer to what you mentioned, Mr. Vasic, earlier on, these statements do not properly fall within Rule 66(A)(ii), as they are not from witnesses in the instant case. The Prosecution disclosed them out of an abundance of caution, I am informed, in case there was any exculpatory material in them. On this point, it was noted by the Prosecution that the Defence request from the last 65 ter meeting for the Prosecution to disclose, if in any doubt, without worrying about the Rule under which the disclosure took place, was more or less being taken in a count being considered by the Prosecution. The interesting development is that I am informed that you were informed that the Prosecution intends to interview some of the Ovcara trial witnesses, with a view to ultimately eventually producing them as witnesses before the Tribunal. Needless to say, I mean the position will change legally if that will be the case. If that happens, the statements that these future witnesses will make, provide to the Prosecution, Prosecutor, will need to be disclosed under Rule 66(A)(ii). I don't think I need to elaborate on this matter. It's clear enough. I think it's satisfactory for you, and I understand that it's clear enough for the Prosecution. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is the position that the Prosecution would take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that basically brings an end -- brings me to the end of the chapter dealing with disclosure, which has been a long one but which is of fundamental importance in the pre-trial stage. We are moving. We are moving slowly, but maybe not at an optimum performance, but I take it that I cannot at the moment -- certainly I cannot pin the blame on the Prosecution, and I don't think I can pin the blame on anyone else for the time being. So hopefully we will progress in this sphere between now and the next Status Conference in a way that will be satisfactory to all. Are there any further comments that any one of you would like to make in the context of disclosure? Disclosure under any of the sections or under any of the Rules that I mentioned, 66, 67, 68. Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The Prosecution has no further issues regarding disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam. Mr. Vasic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We have no new comments. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I see some sign language --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speaking on behalf of all of the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see sign language coming from your colleagues. I'm happy to note that, because that enables me to move to the next item, which is the date for trial, which I am sure is the matter that you are most interested in. No date for trial has as yet been fixed. It doesn't mean to say that we are ignoring the matter or that we are not giving it enough attention. It is anticipated, but again much depends on several other matters, it is anticipated that your trial will start in the first part of 2005. That's if the situation of the Tribunal remains as it is. There could be changes. There could be the burden, the load of the Tribunal could become less, in which case, of course, your case would be advanced. There could be more plea agreements, guilty pleas coming from some of your colleagues detained in Scheveningen. But rebus sic stantibus as matters stand at the moment, it is envisaged that the trial -- we should be able to start the trial in 2005. There will be developments, I suppose, which will impact on this date. And if it will impact on this date, I am sure that it will not impact negatively, but it could only impact positively. So that is the position. I know it doesn't -- that this doesn't make any one of you happy, but I'm afraid that we are not in a position to do anything about it for the time being. Are there any comments on this matter, on this issue? Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I began this case, time meant something to me. The beginning of trial. And if the beginning was put off, that suited me in some way. It would give me more time to prepare for the trial. But in speaking to my client, of course, we both felt that as early a start as possible would be advantageous. But after sharing our thoughts, all of the defence teams believe what was said at the 65 ter Conference about the scheduling. But what you said in a couple of sentences made me a little concerned, Your Honour. First of all, you said that it would start in early 2005 and then you said in 2005. I think these two pieces of information could be interpreted in different ways. I'm speaking, I think, on behalf of all three of the accused that we would all prefer it to be as soon as possible in 2005, and I would be very concerned by the fact if you stand by this other sentence that this would be the -- the trial would be in or during the course of 2005. That would be something that could affect the mood of our clients and our explanation to them about the burdens on the Trial Chamber, as well as the entire Tribunal. First of all, we're speaking in the spirit of the Statute and in the spirit of Articles 20 and 21 when we're talking about our concern for the trial to start as soon as possible. But -- so we would ask you then to clarify for us what you said regarding the trial starting in early 2005 and in 2005. This other sentence is something that is causing somewhat a little bit of concern for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... -- is that there is no fixed date. 2005 is the year in which there will be fresh elections for the -- of the Judges of this Tribunal. 2005 is the year in which the term of office of the current incumbent -- list of incumbent ad litem Judges lapses as well. So I can only say that it is envisaged, it is hoped, that we will be able to start this case in the beginning of 2005. The decision is -- ultimately does not rest with me, as you know. It rests with others, who will take into stock the progress of this pre-trial -- these pre-trial proceedings. The estimate that we will have of the duration of the trial. Any steps that I might take in due course in curtailing, reducing the number of witnesses or establishing a time limit within which the Prosecution, for example, is to finish its case, and same with the Defence. There are many ifs and buts, et cetera. But the thing is this, that our main concern is your main concern, and namely, is to try to give the accused a trial within a reasonable time. A reasonable time, in the context of the circumstances which pertain to the case, and also to the circumstances of the Tribunal. We will do our level best. If we could start it in January -- in December of 2004, I can assure you that we will start it in December of 2004 and we will not wait for 2005. But I cannot then tell you it will definitely start in January of 2005. I could just give one simple explanation of a problem that could arise. Depending on how long this trial will be anticipated to last, we could find ourselves in a position where we would not be able to appoint any ad litem Judges to sit with a permanent Judge, because the term of the ad litem Judges would lapse in the meantime. The term of the permanent Judges will lapse one month after. So we will need to take proper stock of the situation as we go along. There are problems, problems which we are very much determined to surmount, in the interest of each of the accused that is awaiting trial here, particularly those accused who have not benefitted from provisional release. I can assure you that I am fully aware of the situation, that I will do my level best, but I -- of course, I cannot promise a date and a month. And even if I did, it will not be a serious undertaking on my part, knowing what the circumstances and the situation is. But we will do our best. Any further comments on this matter? No. Agreed facts. You know that our Rules also envisage the possibility of the teams, Prosecution and Defence, coming together and agreeing on certain facts. I am fully aware that we are still at a relatively early stage in the proceedings; however, you might, and I would suggest that you might start thinking on this. And I can tell you why. Carrying on the issue that I have just finished dealing with, namely, that the smoother the road that you prepare for the Trial Chamber, and the shorter it is, the earlier we can start and finish the case. So if there are any facts that you could agree upon, then please do sit down and cooperate with one another and come back to us, and we will take notice of them. And it may carry a lot of importance, have an impact on the duration of the case. So I would exhort you to take this -- give this matter your attention, even at this stage, recognising that it is an early stage. But you may be aware of certain facts that you could agree upon. All right? I'm not going to ask for a feedback from any one of you at this stage on this matter, but I will face you again with it in the next Status Conference. Before I address each one of the accused personally on other matters, is there any matter that you would like to raise in addition to what we have been discussing, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The Prosecution has no other matters to raise with you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to initiate a question, but I am afraid that I would need to go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session, having closed this section. Are there any other matters that you would like to raise before I address the accused? I see none. So let's start with you, Mr. Mrksic. I explained to you earlier on that the purpose -- one of the purposes of the Status Conference is to give you an opportunity to raise any matter, any issue relating to your mental and physical condition, as well as your state of detention. Would you like to enter a statement on any of these matters or these issues? THE ACCUSED MRKSIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing to state which I have not said earlier on. Everything is fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radic. THE ACCUSED RADIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no problems. My health is stable. And I thank you for your interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Sljivancanin. THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is the question that is put at all sessions, but I'm saying yet again I do not feel well in prison. It's not because of the staff, the people who work there, because they are very sensible, they carry out their duties as they should, and they make every effort to assist us. I wish to emphasise that I also went to see the doctor, and I must say that I have never been treated better than by those doctors. But also during the past year, I changed my environment three times in prison, which has quite an effect on any person who is trying to find his way in a new environment. But I assume that that is what the Detention Unit does. Since you said everything that you had to say about the trial commencement date, I wish to point out that I came here to defend myself against all the falsehoods about me that were referred to in the indictment. The truth should come out, but it's been a long wait. So I would kindly ask you to start with a trial as soon as possible so that I could speak in my defence and refute these falsehoods. I would like the truth to come out as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Sljivancanin, and I will take your words into account and try and do my best. Any further comments, matter, issues? I see none, or I hear none, which means that I can now bring this Status Conference to an end. My apologies and my thanks at the same time to the interpreters and technical staff. We have been here a full -- we have exceeded our time. My apologies. At the same time, I thank you and I commend you to your superiors for being so cooperative. The next Status Conference will be convened according to the Rules, that is, within 120 days from today. I thank you all, and I declare this Status Conference closed now.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
